To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the consumption of an energy drink, with a high level of sugars and a low level of caffeine, does not improve alertness, and may even worsen sleepiness and performance in people already sleepy, due to a prior period of sleep restriction.

A high sugar content, high caffeine drink does not counteract sleep loss, and may worsen it, as shown by slower RTs and increased lapses during the third 30-min session of a 90-min period of sustained performance.
the ingestion of a high-sugar low caffeine drink does nothing to alleviate sleepiness but might even enhance it.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of a high sugar drink on the alerting and fatigue counteracting properties of caffeine.
the effect of the consumption of energy drinks in the afternoon on subsequent performance.
the effects of energy drinks on performance, and the mechanisms underlying the performance effects, particularly in relation to sleepiness and sleep.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
'Energy drinks' do not alleviate sleepiness and may exacerbate it.

a high sugar content, high caffeine content 'energy drink', when consumed during the afternoon of a sleep restricted night, does not alleviate the sleepiness that results from sleep deprivation, and may worsen it.
a high glucose drink containing a low caffeine content for 'flavour' is ineffective in counteracting sleepiness and may actually exacerbate it.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the ingestion of a high sugar, low caffeine drink in a sleep deprived person, does not alleviate sleep induced sleepiness and may worsen it.
the ingestion of a high glucose drink, containing a low level of caffeine, does not counteract the effects of a sleep loss, but may exacerbate them, at least in the short term.
the energy drink had an initial short acting alerting action, but this was not sustained, and there was an increase in sleepiness and a slowing of RTs.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the energy drink did not alleviate sleepiness, and in the context of our experiment, may have exacerbated it.
energy drinks are no more effective than a placebo at alleviating the effects of sleep deprivation on performance.
energy drinks do not counteract the effects of sleep loss.
